02FD9A23: The Western Cape earns more per visitor than the rest of South Africa. The province takes about a quarter of national foreign spend from about a seventh of the arrivals. Its foreign visitors spend roughly 1.6 times the national average. That is about US$890 per arrival, against US$500 for the rest of South Africa. Foreign direct spend rose 14% in a year, from R22.7 billion in FY2024 to R25.9 billion in FY2025.
2FA3DC05: Domestic travel sits beside this picture. Domestic trips recovered in volume in 2025 but fell in value, with nominal overnight spend down 31.9% to R12.7 billion. This study's mandate and target are international, so domestic trips and spend are tracked as context (section 1.1).
347BF66D: **Conversion.** Six barriers stand between interest and a visit. Distance and cost, safety perceptions and the lack of a reason to travel now keep the trip on the bucket list. Reluctance to self-drive, low awareness beyond Cape Town, the Cape Winelands and the Garden Route and difficulty finding information keep visitors from the rest of the province. The barriers apply all year and in every market, so conversion is the first task.
0206FD3C: Conversion sets the pace all year, and the gateway sets it at the summer peak. The growth model draws three paths from a 2025 base of about 1.5 million. By 2035 the conservative case reaches about 1.8 million, the base case about 2.2 million and the accelerated case about 2.5 million. Chapters 1 to 5 call the last two the base and accelerated cases.
612D97B9: The paths differ by intervention, not by demand potential. The base case assumes Wesgro holds its current effort while Emirates, Qatar, Ethiopian and Turkish Airlines keep adding capacity. The accelerated case also needs direct India and China routes and dedicated activation in India, China, the USA and the Gulf. Without confirmed routes, it reverts to base.
4A627B3D: On the eleven full routes, marketing cannot make up for missing seats, but on the Dubai, Addis Ababa and Doha routes, at 65% to 72% load, it can. The hub markets supply about 30% of the arrivals the base case adds, the largest share of any market group.
3F1EBA1D: The base case implies growth of 3.8% a year and the accelerated case 5.3%, against a global norm of 3% to 5%. Faster growth has been sustained outside a recovery. Santiago's airport grew from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019, at least 5.5% a year. Chile's international seat capacity rose about 40% to 50% from 2013 to 2019. The fastest growers aimed institutions, marketing and air access at one binding constraint. For Chile that constraint was long-haul access. The Western Cape's first constraint is conversion, and seats into one gateway airport pace it at the peak.
59A82B45: **Accelerating tourism growth: towards 2.5 million international arrivals by 2035**
0CF781E2: Base case by group; accelerated not split
58BEB9C3: The table shows the model's arrivals baseline, and the airport count is tracked beside it, from 1.44 million in FY24/25 (section 5.3). The spend target needs the same care. The model's 2024 spend of R27.12 billion sits 19% above the R22.7 billion reported for FY2024, so R40.6 billion is not measured from R25.9 billion. The spend path is to be rebased on the FY2025 actual.
7D21155F: **Arrivals.** The growth model supports 2.2 million to 2.5 million by 2035. From 1,498,829 arrivals in 2025, its base case reaches 2,175,778 by 2035 and its accelerated case 2,516,282, above a conservative case of 1,822,634. The base case holds Wesgro's effort at 2025 intensity, with selective frequency gains and continued hub expansion. The accelerated case needs confirmed direct routes to India and China, above-baseline activation and more hub capacity into Cape Town; without the routes, volume reverts to base. Growth to 2.5 million is that case rounded, and it is the target the report carries.[^5]
50322939: About 1.44 million international visitors arrived through Cape Town International in FY24/25 on the airport's count, against 1.16 million in FY19/20, the last pre-pandemic year. Arrivals passed the pre-pandemic peak of 1.19 million, set in FY18/19, during FY23/24, when they reached 1.36 million. FY25/26 added a further step to 1.57 million.[^12]
75F07A5F: The action plan's task is to move the Western Cape from recovery to growth. The first half is done. On the airport's count, international arrivals through Cape Town International reached 1.44 million in FY24/25 against 1.16 million in FY19/20, and 1.57 million in FY25/26. On South African Tourism's provincial count the province still stood below 2019 in 2025 (Appendix A2).[^18]
60AEEFDA: The action plan aims at 2.5 million international arrivals by 2035, 5.3% a year on the accelerated case and just above the world's norm (sections 1.1 and 2.1). Growth above trend is rare across whole regions; where it happens, it is specific to a destination. Benchmarking asks which deliberate choices let comparable destinations outgrow the world, and which of them the Western Cape can adapt. It looks for how each destination removed what bound its growth, not for isolated good practice.[^39]
20123FA6: The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors. The province has its own precedent above the 5% mark. International two-way passengers at Cape Town International rose from 1.71 million in 2015 to 3.1 million in 2024, about 6.8% a year. Most of the rise came before COVID-19: traffic grew about 11% a year from 2015 to 2019 and about 3.5% a year from 2019 to 2024, inside the norm. The faster years followed the forming of the Cape Town Air Access partnership in 2015. It counts 33 route launches since, and 16 more destinations were served in 2025 than in 2015, close to the 17 mainline routes in the peer comparison above. Outside a recovery, 2015 to 2019 is the province's own case of growth above the norm.[^45]
7C46C3B5: Singapore was chosen for joining air access, service quality, food culture and visitor segmentation in one approach. Its question was how to turn transit through Changi into stays. Its answer is a stopover programme that the tourism board, Changi Airport Group and Singapore Airlines run under one coordinated strategy. It received 16.5 million international visitors in 2024 and record tourism receipts of about S$29 billion. A hotel transformation map and fund lifted quality alongside, moving Singapore from lower-value stopovers towards longer stays and higher spend.[^48]
57E54962: Events do the same work across the calendar, and the Western Cape has the green-season gap they address (section 2.3). The province needs one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Western Cape Government, with conference bidding aligned to sector strengths.[^55]
34C71635: **Objective 7, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes, and objective 15, Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies.** Chile's airport concession and air access fund; New Zealand's route-tied marketing. Cape Town's own international traffic grew about 6.8% a year from 2015 to 2024, most of it before COVID-19.
2F644A12: The fall and the climb were both steep. Arrivals dropped to 80,400 in FY20/21 and 378,500 in FY21/22, then returned to 1.07 million in FY22/23. Two-way international passengers reached 2.90 million in FY24/25, 29% above FY17/18, and 3.3 million in calendar 2025 inside a total of 11.1 million, both up 7% on the year.[^71]
6BAD3812: Foreign direct spend in the province rose from R22.7 billion in FY2024 to R25.9 billion in FY2025, a gain of 14% in one year. The Western Cape earns that spend from a modest share of the national market. Across the four quarters of 2025 it took 16%, 13%, 13% and 16% of South Africa's foreign arrivals and 26%, 20%, 22% and 27% of foreign direct spend.[^73]
18029C07: No other province shown earns spend ahead of its arrivals. Across the same quarters Gauteng took 41% to 44% of arrivals and 39% to 48% of spend, and Mpumalanga 24% to 27% of arrivals and 7% to 9% of spend. Abroad, Morocco drew 17.4 million arrivals and Egypt 15.7 million in 2024, against Kenya's 2.4 million and the province's 1.4 million. Egypt earned US$970 per arrival and Namibia US$250, so arrival growth alone is a weak guide to economic return.[^75]
5E1CAC34: Each added night raises spend and regional reach without an added seat or a peak-hour runway slot. Three levers follow. Extensions can be sold through the safari and tour operators who build the itinerary, with the Cape Winelands, the Whale Coast and the Garden Route as the second leg (objectives 5 and 10). Business-event delegates can add nights before or after an event (objective 2). Singapore's work to turn transit into stays shows a hub pursuing the same gain (section 2.2). The plan tracks average nights in the province by market group as indicator T2-30, with a baseline set from South African Tourism data in 2027.
5B4606F5: Most of these visitors arrive through someone else's hub. The UAE route carried 222,923 air arrivals into Cape Town in 2025, Qatar 126,078, Ethiopia 123,250 and Turkey 89,090. The four hub routes through Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa and Istanbul carried 53% of arrivals on the ten largest routes. The hubs, not the source markets, are therefore the province's working gateways.[^90]
612A4897: Recent arrivals run the other way. Stats SA counted 75,541 Indian and 41,651 Chinese tourists to South Africa in 2024, then 69,680 and 37,902 in 2025. From January to September 2026 the totals were 37,875 from India, down 30.0%, and 22,848 from China, down 23.7%. These are national arrivals by residence, computed from the monthly releases, not provincial counts. Industry views attribute the fall to air access, price and trade confidence as well as entry rules. The model's 8% a year stands as the base case, and the decline is carried as context and risk. The 2027 starting point has not been retested against the decline.
4A230942: Spend follows the mix. The model fixes average spend for each group, from R24,500 a visitor in mature markets to R8,500 in regional ones. On that basis base-case foreign spend rises from a modelled R27.12 billion in 2024 to R40.59 billion in 2035. Volume and value come from different markets.[^105]
1016161E: Spend ranks the markets differently. African visitors spent R4.2 billion in the province in 2025, and Zimbabwe and Namibia supplied R1.94 billion of it. Per visitor the order reverses: Nigerians and Ghanaians spend most, level with mature overseas markets, followed by Angolans and Tanzanians. The volume markets are not the value markets.[^117]
7069F482: Business travel has recovered worldwide and is still growing. Global spend passed its 2019 level of US$1,431 billion in 2024, at US$1,517 billion, and is forecast to reach US$1,782 billion in 2027. China, at US$360.8 billion, and the USA, at US$329.1 billion, led in 2024. Seven of the ten largest markets are Western Cape priority markets. The figures cover all business travel, not business events alone.[^120]
2BA972CA: Business events lift spend and can be scheduled. International business-event delegates to South Africa spend R6,400 a day on average. The CTICC contributed R6.5 billion to the provincial economy and supported 13,000 jobs nationally in FY2024, and it rates international events above local ones for revenue. Events can be dated more freely than leisure trips, and a delegate may stay on, travel into the regions or return on holiday.[^121]
735BD980: The busiest of those routes run full (Figure 2.15). In the year to November 2025, eleven of the 27 routes with load data ran above 80% and sixteen ran at 75% or more, led by Newark and Atlanta (section 2.1). These are averages for the year, so the fullest routes have little room left in the summer peak.[^141]
5551EE77: Two of the airport's seven components are full and four are under strain (Table 2.14). The runway and the domestic arrivals hall, the first thing a visitor connecting through Johannesburg or Durban meets, have reached their limits. The site is boxed in between the runway and the roads, so the fix has to move the runway itself. ACSA's programme of about R11.3 billion targets every problem area, and the risk is timing, not scope. The runway still needs regulatory sign-off and terminals take five to seven years to build, so each peak before relief runs tighter than the last.[^150]
6D181699: George is full today, and its fix is small, funded and near. The airport handled 911,000 two-way passengers in 2025, above the roughly 900,000 its terminal was built for. A R310 million terminal expansion doubles capacity to about 2 million passengers a year by 2028 or 2029, with construction from October 2026. George is a domestic airport, so international visitors connect through another gateway. Reliability is the open risk: fog and wind divert flights, and a lapse in landing-system approvals cancelled more than ten flights in one day in January 2025.[^151]
547B02F6: Cape Winelands Airport stays a scenario, not committed capacity. It is a private development at the old Fisantekraal airfield, some 30 km north of the city, with a first phase of about R8 billion. Its 3.5 km runway could take long-haul aircraft, its terminal is designed for 5.2 million passengers a year and it targets first passengers in 2028. Environmental appeals were dismissed in May 2026, but financial close, aviation licensing and airline commitments are not yet evidenced. Capacity and certainty therefore pull apart: the certain fix comes last, and the earliest large option is the least certain.[^152]
12C1566F: Cruise visits fell back in 2025/26 with no change in berth capacity. The province hosted 70, 67 and 79 vessels in the 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 seasons, carrying 144,125, 109,884 and 127,178 passengers. Wesgro counts 64 cruise liner visits, 106,240 passengers and 37,200 crew for 2025/26. The full study for that season, with unique and international passengers, is not in hand. That season added R1.35 billion to provincial GDP-R from R1.47 billion of spending and supported 1,701 full-time equivalent jobs in the province. The season before, Wesgro counted 79 cruise liner visits and 83 vessel calls, and cruise added R1.79 billion to GDP-R after displacement, with 1,234 direct and 2,345 total jobs.[^154]
7123CABC: Ships come for the circuit, not for one port. A line deploys a ship for a season when a full itinerary works, and Wesgro's prospectus sells Cape Town as the homeport for two. The east coast itinerary calls at Mossel Bay and Hermanus, then at Gqeberha, East London, Durban and Richards Bay. It runs on to Mozambique, the East African coast and the Indian Ocean islands. The west coast itinerary runs through Saldanha Bay and Port Nolloth to Namibia, Angola and St Helena. The province holds one equipped port in that circuit. Mossel Bay handled 21 calls and about 13,000 passengers and opened a R22 million passenger facility in November 2025, yet ships anchor and tender there and only small and mid-sized ships call. Saldanha Bay has had 3 trial calls into an ore terminal, with no cruise berth or passenger facility. Calls therefore rise when the circuit works, not when Cape Town markets harder. Mossel Bay's own count differs: calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season, and the Cruise Economic Contribution Study counts 21 passenger-day visits there in 2024/25, with 31,146 passengers and R46.3 million of spending. For 2025/26 Wesgro counts 13 cruise liner visits across Mossel Bay, Hermanus and Saldanha Bay together, with just over 7,150 passengers and R11.2 million of spending. The counts follow different definitions and are not reconciled.[^156]
50BE08EB: Port capital is not going to cruise. Saldanha's R4 billion upgrade serves iron ore and Cape Town's port project is a container expansion, which leaves the Mossel Bay facility as the only cruise capital in the pipeline. The Infrastructure Report therefore reads cruise growth as a task of demand and product, not of capital works. Mossel Bay reports that its early excursion information was too limited, and that a broader, professionally packaged offer drew more value from each call.[^157]
0DB978A9: Overall readiness halves between the Metro and the periphery. The Cape Metro rates 4.5 out of 5, the Cape Winelands and the Garden Route 3.4, the Overberg 2.7, the West Coast 2.5 and the Central Karoo 1.9. Accessibility falls fastest (Table 2.16), and the six profiles below show what lies behind each rating.[^167]
247D2389: Transport is strong at the scale of the city and weak at the scale of the visit. Most major attractions lie within about an hour of the airport. Unreliable rail and weak last-mile links, most of all in the Metro South-East and on the Cape Flats, keep visitors in cars. The Department of Mobility reports that congestion, including long transfers from airport to hotel, gives visitors a poor arrival. The pipeline exceeds R30 billion: ACSA's programme, the R20 billion V&A Granger Bay expansion, the R3.3 billion MyCiTi Phase 2 and the private Cape Winelands Airport. It leaves last-mile transit to Chapman's Peak, Constantia and Cape Point unfunded. No capital reaches online booking for smaller operators or township tourism.[^169]
71A91173: The N2 is the district's sole transport spine. George Airport adds access and the Outeniqua Choo Tjoe line has heritage potential, but passenger rail is limited and no shuttle links the towns. The Department of Mobility cites the George Integrated Public Transport Network as evidence that affordable, reliable local transport can support tourism in secondary destinations. The pipeline lifts the air bottleneck through the George terminal and a R9.4 million landing-system upgrade. It leaves no international carrier, a deep winter trough and unfunded gaps in transport between nodes and in product at Mossel Bay and George. FEDHASA points to the Discover Garden Route partnership as a platform for a regional proposition. Mossel Bay reports inconsistent restaurant quality and service, and it is expanding roads as demand grows.[^171]
4BEA0980: The district is connected to the outside and disconnected within. The N1, N2 and R44 carry self-drive visitors, yet no public transport links the Stellenbosch, Franschhoek and Paarl triangle. Rail to Stellenbosch suffers vandalism and unreliable service. Franschhoek's Wine Tram shows what a purpose-built service can do, though no other valley has copied it. Transport is the district's lowest category score, at 2.8. The pipeline is the private airport, sited 24 km from Stellenbosch, a wider airport precinct of R16 billion to R20 billion and a provincial drive to bring smaller cellars online. None of it funds transit within the triangle, prices within reach of domestic visitors or product beyond wine.[^173]
7E0B1CEE: Access is by road alone. The R27 and N7 carry almost all visitors, services thin out beyond Langebaan, Vredenburg and Saldanha and the northern municipalities have no passenger rail. Transport, enabling structure and activity attractions are its lowest category scores, at 2.2 each. The pipeline favours freight and harbours: the Transnet upgrade of Saldanha port, the completed R693 million Malmesbury bypass, harbour redevelopment at Lambert's Bay, Elands Bay and Laaiplek and rural broadband. No capital is committed to accommodation or payments infrastructure, and no airport is planned. The municipality adds that products, guesthouses and new hubs are emerging without an organised development strategy.[^175]
41FC93C0: No scheduled visitor transport links the coastal towns. The N2 and R43 carry access, the Cape Town to Caledon rail line is freight only and no public tourism transport connects Hermanus, Stanford, Elim or Agulhas. The district reports that limited reliable transport holds back solo travellers, while seasonal City Sightseeing services have raised traffic. The pipeline is small: the R81.7 million Agulhas lighthouse precinct, a R17 million re-gravelling of the Malgas road and Whale Coast route packaging. It gives the route an eastern anchor but leaves the De Hoop corridor without accommodation investment, and it funds neither online booking nor products for the months outside whale season.[^177]
3F9F9F24: 300 km of coastline fragments the route; no inter-town shuttle
66CF11B2: Attractions cluster along three corridors, and variety falls off beyond them. The Cape corridor holds the most varied base in a compact area, while the Cape Winelands corridor centres narrowly on vineyards and scenery. The N2 corridor delivers outdoor and adventure products, most without interpretation or heritage content. The Overberg and the West Coast hold marine and wildflower assets that the Infrastructure Report finds largely inactive, with no guided tours, interpretation centres or bookable product around them. The Central Karoo and the northern interior have no anchor product.[^186]
2277FB99: Accommodation concentrates in the same three corridors. The Cape corridor has the widest range, skewed to four-star and five-star properties, and the Cape Winelands form a premium cluster with no budget tier. The Garden Route is lined with self-catering units and resorts and is short of the quality-graded hotels that anchor midweek, conference and business travel. Supply thins across the inland Overberg, West Coast and Central Karoo, which leaves no chain of stock for multi-night touring. Two of the report's province-wide claims on accommodation are qualified below.[^187]
1A0FBA7F: Dining and retail narrow fastest outside the core. Most tourism-oriented eateries sit along the Metro's coastal belt, in the Cape Winelands and on the Garden Route's N2 corridor, with Hermanus, Langebaan, Paternoster, Swellendam and Prince Albert as regional dining nodes. Elsewhere large inland areas offer little beyond franchise fast food, and township food economies remain outside mainstream itineraries.[^188]
62406B15: Passenger rail has collapsed as a mode. Trainsets fell from about 110 in 1995 to about 91, pushing some 400,000 commuters onto saturated roads, and congestion in the Metro costs an estimated R2.8 billion a year. Metrorail still runs 460 km, five lines and 104 of 121 stations, with 22.7 million passenger trips in FY2025. No line reaches the airport, the network is rated functionally unusable for tourism and the MyCiTi bus service to the airport remains suspended.[^190]
5BA88D3E: The remedies are named but not scheduled. Four transport enablers are listed, none dated or costed: the Cape Town Integrator, rail restoration and devolution, a high-speed city to airport link and George to Cape Winelands passenger rail. PRASA's R21.1 billion programme and the City's R123 billion, 30-year devolution case cover fleet and lines, and neither carries a tourism product or an airport link.[^195]
4FBAFE1B: Beds are short in particular places, and no bed count yet sizes the gap. The profiles name the places: mid-market stock in the Cape Winelands, hotels and graded inland stock on the West Coast and the country east of Hermanus. On the West Coast overnight stays remain below the provincial average. The Infrastructure Report goes further and maps no mid-scale branded product anywhere between luxury estates and basic self-catering, a claim this report does not carry across the province.[^196]
232DE45C: Beyond the Metro the province has the assets, and the task is to turn them into complete, accessible visits. The Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg have product and need transport between towns, packaging and service depth to lengthen stays. The West Coast and the Central Karoo show that distinct assets are not enough where services, mobility and year-round demand stay weak. Transport is a problem of connection and dispersal, not a province-wide shortage of capacity.[^204]
069B9FCF: **Objective 10, Support diversified route and product development, and objective 11, Align visitor experience in-destination.** One of six touring routes rates Ready, and every district outside the Metro is outpaced by its own assets. The gaps differ by place: transfers in the Cape Winelands, depth east of Hermanus, beds and year-round product on the West Coast and services along Route 62. The mid-market gap is a product question to test place by place. Nine of the ten places international tourists visit most are in the Metro.
58436F8E: Wesgro works on the demand side through six units: Cape Town Air Access, Cruise Cape Town, the Convention Bureau, Destination Marketing, Research and Tourism. Around them sit fifteen external organisations across three tiers of government and industry. Cape Town Air Access is itself a partnership, formed in 2015, of the City of Cape Town, the provincial government, ACSA, Cape Town Tourism, South African Tourism, Wesgro and the private sector. This report is Wesgro's plan and cannot bind the other bodies, so it describes each by its interest and the levers it holds.[^205]
7208A055: Alignment across those tiers is thin. Stakeholders described strain at SA Tourism and a lack of fiscal space. More than twenty bodies produce tourism data, yet the Diagnostic finds no single view of visitor behaviour, which leaves strategy reacting rather than predicting. The Department of Mobility reports the same split in its own field: mobility responsibilities are spread across the three tiers, and local governments often lack the capacity and funding to carry them out. Both insights are rated High.[^207]
17D631EE: The summary describes a system short of capacity, money and data. Mandates are fragmented across the three tiers, municipal delivery capacity is uneven and weak or expired partnerships limit implementation. Funding sits below what the growth ambition requires, most of all for destination management, marketing and mobility. The data architecture is too fragmented, lagged and proxy-based to give a reliable provincial view of visitor volumes, spend, spread or economic impact. Community, township and village operators often lack the market readiness, compliance capability and digital skills to reach formal demand channels. Crime perceptions cut across transport, township tourism and international selling; section 2.1 ranks safety among the conversion barriers. Skills insights sit under other themes.[^210]
62A2F41F: The forums serve marketing better than development. The West Coast District Municipality reports that provincial and regional forums are dominated by destination marketing, and that provincial support, Wesgro's strategy and district needs are poorly matched on grants, capacity building and skills. Both insights are rated High. Where the task is selling, collaboration is reported to work: the CTICC describes effective joint bidding, and !Khwa ttu markets itself through LTOs, community partners and content creators.[^227]
4C7921A2: Activity figures are not crime rates. The City records 2,895 motorist assists by N2 patrols from September 2024 to January 2026, 1,061 of them camera-detected, and 80% of highway incidents since July 2025 were answered within five minutes. SANParks appointed a visitor-safety manager for Table Mountain in December 2025, yet a robbery on Lion's Head in October 2026 prompted a public dispute over patrol coverage. Tourism Monitors figures count people trained, not people placed. SAPS retains command, and the Western Cape Government holds oversight under section 206 of the Constitution.
7D9CAF29: Foreign visitors spent R25.9 billion in the province in FY2025, but little of it reaches its townships and rural settlements. The 20 shortlisted communities come from a long-list of every Census sub-place cluster of 1,500 people or more with official unemployment of 25% or more. Named mission, fishing and farm settlements are added. That gives 107 communities holding 2.81 million people in 2011, 48% of the province. Five weighted criteria (need, tourism potential, proximity, readiness and access) produce the shortlist of 20, five in the Cape Metro and three in each district.[^234]
7EF8A8F5: The 20 hold 18.4% of the province's residents and 15.4% of employed residents (Census 2011), yet receive 0.02% to 0.04% of foreign direct spend. This comes to about R4 million to R10 million a year on the documented floor, against R259 million a year if they captured 1% of FY2025 foreign direct spend.[^235]
1D4FBC07: **Objective 13, Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion.** The binding constraint is a seller with a stake, then a safe way in, then demand pulled from the adjacent node. Circular 131 interrupted established municipal funding of LTOs and leaves the contracted-services route open.
21465511: Goal 1 sets out to break through three ceilings on demand, in markets, seasons and spread, by reshaping the brand towards new traveller segments. Five markets supplied 63% of overseas arrivals in 2025, and the UK, Germany and the USA supplied 52% between them. June held 6.4% of the year's international seats at Cape Town International in 2025, against 10.8% in December. Beyond the core routes, named experiences reach the visitor through day tours, walk-ins and local permits more often than through an online ticket.[^246]
64EA31AA: Goal 1 carries most of the base case. Between 2025 and 2035 the base case adds 676,949 arrivals. The four hub markets, the UAE, Qatar, Ethiopia and Turkey, supply 206,584 of them and the mature markets 178,780. The acceleration markets, led by India and China, supply 175,818, regional Africa 110,298 and the strategic group 5,469. Conversion comes first and seats pace it at the peak, so the air access objective in Goal 2 runs beside this goal from the first phase (objective 7). The growth model's 1.8 million seat figure marks 2025 capacity, which airlines have extended since. The goal is judged on arrivals by market group, foreign direct spend and green-season nights and share, not on arrivals alone (section 5.2).[^248]
31B4A6B6: **Initiative I1**, segment-led activation and yield in mature markets, carries this entry with objective 5 (section 4.3). **Indicators** T1-01 international arrivals, T1-02 arrivals by market group and T1-03 foreign direct spend at impact level, with T2-01 segment home-market arrivals at outcome level. T3-38, regional test offers with completed regional bookings, measures the output (section 5.2). A regional stop on a city day tour does not count; a completed regional booking does. The awareness research runs through I16.
05307F88: The shared strategy and the count come first, in 2027. Wesgro agrees one event acquisition and calendar strategy with the Convention Bureau, the City and the Western Cape Government. The calendar strategy builds on the year-round promotion and MICE marketing in the City's framework for 2019 to 2024. Wesgro also sets up a way to measure meetings, incentives and exhibitions. It builds one monthly baseline of sold and available room nights, so that absolute winter nights and revenue are tracked beside the seasonal share. Without that count, no one can tell whether the calendar fills the trough. It then publishes the calendar and aims bids at May to August first (section 4.3).[^262]
6497DEEB: Agree one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Western Cape Government
1BDF7519: Wesgro should run India and China as conversion markets through the hubs and as relationship markets for the direct route. The money shifts towards trade-led conversion rather than broad awareness. India needs early relationships with its carriers and authorities. China is a long-term investment in which awareness and indirect volume come before any non-stop service. By November 2025 Cape Town Air Access had held talks with Cathay Pacific, China Southern, Air India and IndiGo.[^276]
5B53936D: Length of stay is the second yield lever. About a third of North American, German and French visitors to South Africa travel to more than one province, and most multi-province travellers take in wildlife (section 2.3). Wesgro should sell extensions through the operators who build those itineraries, starting with the US and UK trade. The offer is two or three more nights in the Cape Winelands, on the Whale Coast or on the Garden Route, packaged as an add-on with its transfer (objective 10). Each added night raises spend without an added seat or a peak-hour runway slot.[^284]
6E94A34C: **Initiative I1**, segment-led activation and yield in mature markets (section 4.3), with the frequency case run under **I6** (objective 7). **Indicators** T1-03 foreign direct spend at impact level and T2-07 mature-market spend per visitor at outcome level (section 5.2).
5E7C6127: Model correlated hub-closure scenarios with flown-seat and itinerary data by hub, and weight route work towards routings outside any one region
21B4F264: Cruise has room to grow at the berth Cape Town already has. The equipped berth can take 150 or more calls a season; it handled 83 in 2024/25, and the province received 64 cruise liner visits in 2025/26. The 2025/26 season brought R1.47 billion of spending and added R1.35 billion to provincial GDP-R, against about R1.79 billion after displacement a season earlier. The berth is therefore not what limits growth.[^307]
35C3B454: International passengers drive the value (section 2.4). In 2024/25, the last season with a full study in hand, world cruises made up 42 of the 79 vessel visits, and their passengers added R802 million to provincial GDP-R, 73% of what all passengers added. That season also earned R1.326 billion of net foreign exchange and R259 million in taxes. In 2025/26 cruise generated about R1 billion of foreign exchange.[^308]
2FE9D7BA: The regional circuit decides whether ships come. A line commits a ship to Southern Africa for a season only when the whole itinerary works. Cape Town is the homeport, with calls east towards the Indian Ocean islands and west towards Angola and St Helena (section 2.4). The province holds one equipped port in that circuit, and Mossel Bay and Saldanha Bay can extend it east and west. Stakeholders name home porting and expedition vessels as the segments that bring longer stays and higher local spend.[^309]
3905D2E9: Shore capacity decides what a call is worth (section 2.4). On call days passengers converge on flagship sites that are already full in season, and the terminal queues about ten coaches at a time. The berth itself takes ships of up to 300m, the South-Easter delays berthing and there is no shore power. Port capital goes to freight: Saldanha's R4 billion iron-ore expansion and Cape Town's container expansion add no cruise capacity.[^310]
3D969101: Mossel Bay calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season through closer coordination and better excursion packaging, with Wesgro credited
6FE3B676: The best precedent is local. On its own count, Mossel Bay's calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season, supported by closer coordination and better excursion packaging. The town credits its partnership with Wesgro. No benchmark destination offers a cruise precedent, so the case rests on Mossel Bay. The condition is that ship deployments hold. Growth to 2024/25 leaned on Red Sea reroutes, and their reversal is the main risk. Visits fell from 79 to 64 in 2025/26.[^314]
0F8594F0: The growth case needs visitors the current offer serves poorly. The gap in the middle of the accommodation market is a product question, not a province-wide absence. In the Cape Winelands, mid-market stock is effectively absent outside Stellenbosch and a luxury-skewed product mix excludes mid-market and family segments. The Garden Route is described as short of quality-graded hotels that anchor midweek, conference or business travel, yet George already has a branded, conference-capable hotel of 109 rooms. What is missing is a configuration, price point, location or capacity, and it differs by place.[^332]
49C0A266: Two themes and eight objectives carry the goal. The first theme, investment, inclusion and sustainability, settles who benefits from growth, how it is paid for and how it lasts. It gives community product a local seller, keeps LTOs in service, holds growth within what each destination can carry and builds an investment pipeline that follows demand (objectives 13 to 15). The second theme, governance and leadership, settles who decides and who measures. It aligns the three tiers of government, turns industry forums into one joint plan and agrees how data is shared (objectives 16 to 18). The same theme holds two further objectives. Objective 19 takes the national deficits in infrastructure, visas and safety to the tier that holds them. Objective 20 commissions the labour analysis a skills plan will rest on.
4043CC13: By 2035 the goal must leave the province able to deliver its growth and share it. Visitor spend should reach the communities, measured against a reference point of 1% of foreign direct spend, R259 million a year at FY2025 levels (section 5.3). Local tourism bodies should hold stable funding, and tourism projects should reach financial close. The national tier should answer the province's asks, and the province should count its own tourism jobs and spend. Initiatives I12 to I18 carry the eight objectives, with objectives 16 and 17 sharing one forum in I15 (section 4.1).
541553D6: Community inclusion decides whether growth to 2035 is shared. Inclusion here means visitor activity inside the community: a tour, a meal, a bed or a market. A resident commuting to a hotel job in town counts for little or nothing. On that measure the province starts near zero. Foreign visitors spent R25.9 billion in FY2025, and the 20 shortlisted communities received a documented floor of R4 million to R10 million of it.[^347]
513E0FA9: The prize is large. At 1% of FY2025 foreign direct spend, the 20 communities would receive R259 million a year; at 1% of the 2035 spend ambition, R547 million. Both are reference points, not adopted targets (section 5.3). The visitors are already close, and organisation rather than distance keeps their spend out (section 2.5).[^348]
4994EA7E: LTO contracts and budgets are weighted towards destination marketing, leaving little for tourism development (West Coast District Municipality)
08D31A10: The response divides into three tasks that are often run as one (section 2.5). Adaptation and continuity keep a destination trading through a flood or a fire season. Ordinary resource and ecological capacity sets how many visitors a node can carry in a normal year. Emissions mitigation is a third task with its own measures. The LTOs that would help manage the response are fragile, and their funding route sits under objective 13.[^359]
541952DF: The register turns scattered losses into decisions. Some losses already carry a figure: weather cancellations cost Robben Island roughly R16 million a year, and the Meiringspoort rebuild costs R421 million. Once losses are dated and costed by site, Wesgro can route itineraries around a closure and operators can weigh resilience spending against the loss it avoids. Readiness assessments work on the other half. They stop public promotion from sending visitors to a node whose water, power or sites cannot carry them.[^363]
7733E5B5: The evidence agrees on the problem and is thin on the fix. What is needed is a shared growth agenda with clear decision rights and joint delivery plans. No source maps decision rights by tier beyond one summary table. The national tier is barely heard: the Department of Tourism and Stats SA spoke only to data, and SA Tourism has no recorded view. The first task is therefore to hear the national tier directly and write down who decides what. For the districts, one design is already on record. The Tourism Blueprint 2030 recommends tourism coordination at district level, with regional tourism organisations run as non-profits, funded by district municipalities and seating the LTOs. It also asks for the LTO model to be set in law. The Blueprint's targets were set before COVID-19, so this action plan treats its model as a position to test, not a settled design. The mandate settlement below and the LTO service agreements in objective 13 test it against Circular 131.[^372]
48331E77: Joint work already pays where the task is concrete. Mossel Bay's cruise calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season, supported by closer coordination and better excursion packaging. The town credits its public-private tourism model with faster decisions. The CTICC finds the same on bids: destination stakeholders collaborate effectively on bid development and international event attraction.[^378]
1656B4A0: Measuring what the plan sets out to grow is the first data task. Provincial tourism GDP and jobs need a method (section 2.5), and the Department of Tourism adds that official tourism GDP and employment data have lagged since pandemic-era method changes. The Department of Economic Development and Tourism puts tourism at R28.6 billion in gross value added and over 257,000 jobs supported in 2023, with no published method. Data sharing draws more stakeholder insights than any other theme, as section 2.5 shows. Bodies from Stats SA and SA Tourism to ACSA, the airlines and the card schemes produce tourism data. Yet they collect different metrics at different frequencies with different definitions.[^385]
4467939C: Provincial tourism GDP and jobs await an approved method (section 2.5); official data lag after pandemic-era method changes, and the tourism satellite account is slowed by 749 Stats SA vacancies (Department of Tourism)
75B9AD44: The growth model sets out three paths from the 2025 base of 1,498,829 arrivals: 1,822,634 in 2035 on the conservative case, 2,175,778 on the base case and 2,516,282 on the accelerated case. The paths differ by intervention, not by demand potential. Each step of the growth case therefore rests on a named set of interventions. The first two steps draw on Goals 1 and 2 alone. Goal 3 adds arrivals only on the third step, through the three-tier agenda and national escalation (objectives 16 and 19). Its other six objectives decide whether growth is shared, funded, sustained and measured.[^411]
6F390256: The conservative case, 1,822,634 arrivals in 2035, holds existing air access with no added frequencies or routes and continues trade and marketing, with growth in the mature markets and current corridors. Objectives 5 and 7 hold that base. The base case adds 353,144 arrivals to reach 2,175,778. It assumes Wesgro's trade and marketing continue at 2025 intensity while Emirates, Qatar, Ethiopian and Turkish Airlines add frequency and capacity, and India, China and regional Africa grow through hub connections. Objectives 1 to 7, 9 and 10 hold it. The accelerated case adds a further 340,504 to reach 2,516,282. It needs direct India and China routes secured and dedicated activation in India, China, the USA and the GCC, with India, China and the Middle East growing ahead of their source markets. Objectives 4, 7, 16 and 19 deliver it on top of the base.[^412]
304394E4: **If the seat work slips, growth flattens.** The conservative case, with no new seats, ends at 1.82 million in 2035. Projected growth cannot be realised without added capacity or frequency, and without confirmed routes the accelerated case reverts to base. On the full routes, demand work alone cannot close the gap, because carriers are expected to raise fares before they add seats. On the hub routes and in the green season, which have seats to spare, it can.[^415]
7EE427F2: Seven levels run from the vision to the measures, and each has a fixed count in this plan. One vision says where the province is going: grow international arrivals from 1.5 million in 2025 towards 2.5 million by 2035. Three goals say what must change, such as Reshape demand. Six themes say in which part of the system, such as source market growth and diversification. Twenty objectives say where the evidence says to act, such as Convert India and China hub traffic. Eighteen initiatives say what Wesgro and its partners do, such as I4 India and China hub conversion. The 146 actions say who does what, by tier, such as activation inside Xiaohongshu, Douyin and MakeMyTrip. The indicators, 8 at impact, 31 at outcome and 41 at output level, say how Steerco knows, such as T2-06 India and China hub arrivals. The counts come from Chapter 3, the action tables and the traceability table in Appendix A1.
3EAA801F: Phase 2 scales what Phase 1 proved. Hub conversion, regional Africa and segment marketing run at scale. Corridor mobility and product move from design to delivery, on the Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg first. The quality charter is adopted and phased by district, and the investment pipeline reaches financial close on its first projects. Flow management extends beyond the two pilot sites where the pilots held, and the safety pathway widens if the 2028 review supports it. The mid-term review in 2030 tests seat growth against the path the target requires, and checks that the runway is on its published dates (section 5.6).
6D9E6D54: Segment research refreshed; budget shifted towards the segments and markets with the highest yield.
4F7047A9: Agree (2027): convene the stakeholders and agree roles and accountabilities. Design (2027): one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Western Cape Government, building on the MICE and events marketing the City's framework proposed, if it still runs; a way to measure meetings, incentives and exhibitions; one monthly green-season baseline of sold and available room nights by region and type; sales organised by buyer type; one common appraisal, at full public cost, for every publicly supported event. Implement (2028): publish the calendar; aim bids at May to August first; dated offers for named low-demand weeks with airlines and trade, with buyer commitments before public support; cooler-season incentive packages for Indian and Gulf planners.
1A82C0BA: **Crowding in capital.** The rule for capital is the Inclusion Plan's: invest after demand is shown, and attach a maintenance and marketing covenant to any public asset. Wesgro's investment promotion work builds the tourism pipeline from the Infrastructure Report's gap-closure tables, where every district lists tourism gaps with no committed capital (I14). Route support runs through the Cape Town Air Access partnership, scaled and re-termed with public and private money (I6). Its funders already sit in the partnership: the City, the province, ACSA, Cape Town Tourism, SA Tourism, Wesgro and private-sector partners. Its support carries resilience conditions, from tapering and matched airline marketing to clawbacks (objective 7). Corridor mobility (I8) bids into the provincial transport budget; the draft land transport framework allocates R22.8 billion to transport initiatives in the 2024 MTEF. The same framework plans a tourist levy case, which I14 would widen to cover destination management.[^420]
5BC7FAC7: Seat growth against the path the target requires (T2-09, T2-10); arrivals against the base case (T1-01); peak-hour runway headroom; runway on its published dates; green-season nights and share (T1-05)
56CDB39E: Arrivals carry targets on both paths; spend carries the working analysis's base case; jobs, GDP contribution and the other Tier 1 indicators set baselines first.
